title: Fallacies and Pitfalls
summary: Calculate end-to-end pipeline speedup under Amdahl's Law when optimizing individual ML system components.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Calculate end-to-end pipeline speedup under Amdahl's Law when optimizing individual ML system components
- Analyze the fallacies of relying exclusively on benchmark accuracy to assess production readiness
- Explain why traditional CI/CD pipelines cannot detect silent degradation in deployed ML systems
- Evaluate model selection trade-offs between incremental accuracy gains and production execution budgets

blocks.source: Vol I, Introduction, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: Every chapter in this book closes with a section like this one. A **fallacy** is a belief that sounds right but is false, a **pitfall** is a practice that is easy to fall into and costly to recover from, and each entry corrects the mistake with evidence from the chapter.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md: Pay attention to: Amdahl's law pitfall in ML inference pipelines; benchmark fallacy vs production distribution shift; deploy once fallacy and silent drift; algorithmic superiority fallacy vs latency budgets.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Why can code and infrastructure checks in a standard CI/CD pipeline fail to detect a loss of predictive quality, and how should drift and outcome monitoring guide the response?
blocks.md: Compilation, unit tests, and container health can remain healthy while the operating population changes and predictive quality falls. Drift monitoring warns that the input distribution has changed; outcome measurements establish whether relevant quality has declined. Engineers then diagnose the cause and select a repair, which may involve the pipeline, data, model, or deployment requirements. Neither degradation nor retraining follows inevitably from a drift signal.

questions.q: An inference pipeline consists of three sequential stages: data preprocessing taking 60 ms, model inference taking 45 ms, and output postprocessing taking 25 ms (total latency = 130 ms). An engineering team applies kernel fusion and quantization to achieve a \$3× speedup on the model inference stage alone (reducing it from 45 ms to 15 ms). What is the resulting end-to-end pipeline latency and approximate overall system speedup, and what principle does this demonstrate?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. Total initial time is \$60 + 45 + 25 = 130\text{ ms}$. With a \$3\times$ speedup on inference alone (\$45 / 3 = 15\text{ ms}$), the new total latency is \$60 + 15 + 25 = 100\text{ ms}$. The overall speedup is \$130 / 100 = 1.30\times$, representing a 23% overall latency reduction $(1 - 1/1.30 = 0.231)$. This is a classic demonstration of Amdahl's Law: because the inference component accounted for only \$45/130 \approx 34.6\%$ of total execution time, even a dramatic \$3\times$ component improvement yields a modest 23% end-to-end gain. Assuming a \$3\times$ overall pipeline speedup commits the pitfall of ignoring system interactions.
questions.hint: Think about: calculate end-to-end pipeline speedup under Amdahl's Law when optimizing individual ML system components.
options: New latency is 100 ms (an overall speedup of $\approx 1.30\times$, or a 23% reduction in execution time), illustrating Amdahl's Law that component-level speedups yield only marginal end-to-end gains when non-optimized stages dominate.
New latency is 43.3 ms (a \$3.0× overall speedup, or 67% reduction), illustrating linear speedup scaling across modular microservices.
New latency is 15 ms, illustrating that hardware acceleration bypasses pre- and post-processing stages.
New latency is 115 ms, illustrating that quantization overhead cancels out inference gains.

questions.q: Why does high accuracy on curated benchmark datasets (such as ImageNet or GLUE) frequently fail to guarantee production readiness in real-world deployments?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. Curated benchmarks evaluate accuracy on fixed, preprocessed test distributions in unconstrained compute environments. Production deployments encounter domain shifts, slang, sensor noise, demographic variations, strict real-time latency budgets, and hardware precision/memory constraints that offline benchmarks never capture. Explanations regarding CPU execution, synthetic benchmark data, or weight erasure during export are factually inaccurate.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze the fallacies of relying exclusively on benchmark accuracy to assess production readiness.
options: Benchmarks are evaluated on GPUs, whereas all production models run on CPUs.
Benchmark datasets contain only synthetic, computer-generated data that lacks realistic labels.
Neural networks automatically lose their learned weights when exported to production formats.

Benchmarks evaluate models on static, clean distributions without operational constraints (e.g., sub-100 ms latency budgets, memory limits, noise, and ongoing distribution shift), whereas production systems face uncurated edge cases, shifting user behavior, and hardware precision limits.

questions.q: In production ML systems engineering, selecting a model that provides a 1% higher benchmark accuracy is always preferable, even if it requires doubling inference latency and memory footprint beyond the client application's SLA.
questions.explanation: False. Production model selection is a constrained multi-objective optimization problem where task accuracy must be balanced against latency, memory, power, and cost budgets; a model that violates a real-time SLA has effectively zero utility regardless of its benchmark accuracy.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate model selection trade-offs between incremental accuracy gains and production execution budgets.
